post.title: Hurricane Protection Terms Every Florida Homeowner Should Know
post.excerpt: Shopping for hurricane protection in South Florida? This plain-English glossary explains NOA, design pressure, impact ratings, and other key terms before you buy.

sections.text: If you have started shopping for impact windows or shutters in South Florida, you have probably run into a wall of jargon: NOA, design pressure, large missile rating, wind-borne debris region. This glossary breaks down the terms you will actually encounter, in plain English, so you can compare quotes with confidence. When a salesperson uses one of these terms, you will know exactly what they mean and what questions to ask next. Understanding this vocabulary is the single fastest way to become a smarter buyer.

A Notice of Acceptance is Miami-Dade County's product certification. It means the exact product configuration was independently tested and approved for use in the most demanding wind zone in the country. When a contractor says a product is Miami-Dade approved, ask for the NOA number and verify it covers the size being installed. The NOA also spells out the exact anchoring method the installer must follow, which is what your inspector checks against during the final inspection of the work.

Design pressure measures how much wind load a window or door can withstand, expressed in pounds per square foot as positive and negative values. Your home's location, height, and opening sizes determine the DP rating each opening requires. A product that is fine for a ground-floor window inland may not qualify for a top-floor corner opening near the coast, which is why a professional assessment of every opening matters before any quote is final.
Large and Small Missile Impact Ratings

items: Large missile test: the product must survive a nine-pound piece of lumber fired at roughly 50 feet per second, simulating flying debris
Small missile test: the product must survive impacts from small projectiles like roof gravel, required for openings above 30 feet
After impact, the product must still resist thousands of cycles of positive and negative wind pressure
Both window and frame must pass together as an assembly, not as separate parts

sections.text: The Florida Building Code designates areas where flying debris is a proven hazard during storms. Essentially all of Broward, Miami-Dade, and coastal Palm Beach County fall inside it. Inside this region, replacement windows and doors must either be impact rated or be protected by an approved shutter system. This is why a standard non-rated window that is legal in central Florida cannot be installed in most of South Florida.

Impact glass is two panes bonded to a clear structural interlayer. When debris strikes, the glass may crack but stays attached to the interlayer and the frame, keeping the building envelope sealed. Thicker interlayers generally mean better performance and better sound reduction, which is why two impact windows that look identical can perform and cost differently. Ask every bidder what interlayer thickness their quote includes so you can compare like for like.
Permits, Inspections, and Why They Protect You

Every window and door replacement in Florida requires a building permit, and hurricane protection products are no exception. The permit is not red tape: it is how the county verifies that the product being installed matches its approval documents and that the anchoring follows the tested method. A final inspection closes the permit and creates a public record that protects you when you sell the home or file an insurance claim. If a contractor offers to skip the permit to save money, treat it as a serious warning sign and get another bid.
Wind Mitigation and Your Insurance Paperwork

Once your openings are protected, a licensed inspector can complete Florida's uniform wind mitigation form documenting the upgrade. Insurers use that form to apply credits to the wind portion of your premium, and discounts typically depend on whether every opening in the home is protected rather than just some of them. Keep your NOA numbers, permit records, and final inspection approval together in one folder — your inspector and your insurance agent will ask for all three.
How to Use These Terms When Comparing Quotes

items: Ask for the NOA number for every product on the quote and confirm it matches your opening sizes
Confirm the DP rating specified for each opening, not just a blanket number for the house
Check whether pricing is based on the same glass makeup and interlayer across all bids
Confirm the permit and inspection are included in the price and handled by the contractor
